items.elicits: Chooses and executes a comparison strategy (common denominator, benchmark, or visual model) for 3/4 vs 5/8 and states a one-line reason supporting the chosen symbol.
Chooses and executes a comparison strategy for 2/3 vs 7/12 (a pair where a half-benchmark alone does not resolve the comparison, pushing toward a finer method) and justifies the symbol.
Chooses and executes a comparison strategy for 5/6 vs 8/9 (a near-whole pair suited to a distance-from-one benchmark or common denominator) and justifies the symbol.

claims.supports: Under proctored, individual, no-outside-resource conditions with numbers the student could not have prepared, a teacher may conclude the student can independently select and correctly execute a valid strategy (common denominator, benchmark, or visual model) to compare two unlike fractions and can state a one-line reason tied to that strategy that supports the resulting symbol, across three differently-structured fraction pairs.
does_not_support: Does not confirm the student can compare fraction pairs with structures unlike these three (e.g. widely differing magnitudes, or a three-way ordering task).

Does not by itself guarantee the written reasoning names the controlling feature of the chosen strategy rather than restating the answer; that depends on how the 'show how you know' line is scored, which is not specified in the assessment.

Adjacent claim risk: because a common-denominator strategy is explicitly offered as one comparison option, a right symbol with common-denominator work shown here can look like G5C2core evidence, but strategy CHOICE (G5C1) and common-denominator MECHANICS (G5C2core) are different constructs and should not be scored as interchangeable.

A correct symbol with incomplete or incoherent shown work should not be read as full evidence of the claim; the assessment requires work to be shown, but nothing in the artifact specifies that credit depends on the reasoning line being coherent, not just present.

delegation.reason: The comparison and its justification must be produced live, in the room, on paper, with no permitted AI or resource beyond pencil and paper, so the submitted strategy and reasoning reflect the student's own work.

components.component: Chooses a valid strategy from more than one option (not mandated by the item)
components.evidence: Items 1-3 instruct 'show how you know (a common denominator, a picture, or a benchmark like 1/2)' without mandating which, and the three pairs suit different approaches.

components.component: Executes the chosen strategy with computational/graphical accuracy
components.evidence: Each pair requires carrying out the chosen method (e.g. finding equivalent fractions, drawing an accurate model) to arrive at a symbol.
Each item explicitly asks the student to write <, >, or =.

components.component: States a one-line reason connecting the method to the symbol
components.evidence: 'Then show how you know' requires an explicit justification line tied to the shown work, not free-standing prose.

gate1_components.why: Every observable component of G5C1 (strategy choice, execution, correct symbol, and a reasoning line) is already exercised across items 1-3 under supervised conditions; nothing is absent to carry forward.

gate2_materiality.why: Not reached: Gate 1 found no absent component.

gate3_value.why: Not reached: Gate 1 found no absent component.

claims.why_no_intervention: Gate 1 failed: all components of G5C1 are already exercised by items 1-3; there is no absent component to justify adding an item.

items.elicits: Constructs a common denominator for 1/2 and 1/3, converts both to like-sized twelfths... sixths, and adds the resulting numerators.
Constructs a common denominator for 5/6 and 1/4, converts both to twelfths, and subtracts the resulting numerators.

Constructs a common denominator for the fractional parts of two mixed numbers (1/3 and 3/4), converts both to twelfths, and adds the resulting like-sized parts (in addition to combining the whole-number parts).
Translates a word problem into an addition of two unlike fractions (3/4 and 5/6), constructs a common denominator, and combines the resulting like-sized parts.
Translates a word problem into a subtraction of two unlike fractions (2/3 and 1/4), constructs a common denominator, and combines (subtracts) the resulting like-sized parts.

claims.supports: Under these supervised, novel-number conditions, a teacher may conclude the student can independently construct a common denominator, convert two unlike fractions to equivalent like-sized fractions, and correctly combine (add or subtract) the resulting numerators, including inside mixed-number and word-problem contexts.
does_not_support: Does not guarantee evidence that the same common-denominator technique was used in the comparison context (Part A), since items 1-3 explicitly permit a benchmark or visual model instead, so a student could complete the whole assessment without ever using common denominators to compare.

Does not by itself separate a common-denominator-construction error from a plain arithmetic slip in the final add/subtract step; both are bundled into one 'show every step' response unless scored against a rubric that isolates the steps.

Items 4 and 5 alone (non-mixed, non-improper results) do not reach the mixed-number or improper-result handling that G5C2b covers; that evidence comes from items 6 and 7, not from this component in isolation.

Does not confirm efficiency (using the LEAST common denominator) since any valid common multiple produces a correct answer; a correct response via a larger common denominator is still valid evidence of this claim but should not be read as evidence of efficient strategy selection.

delegation.reason: Proctored, individual, paper/pencil-only, AI-prohibited conditions plus the 'show every step' requirement make it implausible for this multi-step work to be produced without the student doing it.

components.component: Finds a correct common denominator (equivalent-fraction construction)
components.evidence: Each item requires converting two unlike fractions to a shared denominator before combining them.

components.component: Converts each fraction correctly to that common denominator
components.evidence: The equivalent-fraction conversion is a required intermediate step in every combine item.

components.component: Correctly adds or subtracts the resulting like-sized numerators (combines)
components.evidence: Each item's final step is adding or subtracting the converted numerators.

components.component: Applies the common-denominator technique specifically in a comparison context (compares)
components.evidence: Items 1-3 explicitly offer 'a common denominator, a picture, or a benchmark' as equally valid strategies, so the assessment's own design does not require the common-denominator method to be used when comparing; that strategy choice is G5C1's territory.

gate1_components.why: The only unexercised component is using common-denominator construction specifically for comparison, but G5C2core's wording is disjunctive ('combines OR compares') and is already carried in substance by the five robust combine items (4-8); Part A deliberately leaves comparison strategy open, which is G5C1's scope, not a gap here.

gate2_materiality.why: Not reached: Gate 1 found no component whose absence narrows support.

gate3_value.why: Not reached: Gate 1 found no component whose absence narrows support.

claims.why_no_intervention: Gate 1 failed: the disjunctive claim is already carried by the combine evidence in items 4-8; the unexercised 'compares' branch is optional by the assessment's own design and belongs to G5C1, not to a gap in this claim.

claims.supports: Under these conditions, this assessment licenses no conclusion about whether the student can simplify a reducible fraction result, because none of the items' correct answers are actually reducible.
does_not_support: Does not confirm the student can recognize when a numerator and denominator share a common factor greater than 1, since none of the assessment's correct results (5/6, 7/12, 1 1/12, 1 7/12, 5/12) present that case.
Does not confirm the student can carry out the divide-by-common-factor reduction procedure itself.
A fully correct paper (every answer matching the key) provides no information on this skill and should not be read by the teacher as evidence that simplification is mastered.
Cannot distinguish a student who would correctly simplify if the case arose from one who would not, since the instrument never presents the case.

delegation.reason: Supervision, individual work, and paper/pencil/no-AI conditions would rule out outside production of any simplification work if it occurred, but this is moot here: no item's correct result requires the reduction step, so there is no submitted evidence of this skill to evaluate.

claims.gap_statement: We cannot tell from this assessment whether the student can simplify a fraction result to lowest terms, because none of the items' correct sums or differences (5/6, 7/12, 1 1/12, 1 7/12, 5/12) share a common factor to reduce, so the skill named in G5C2a is never actually called upon despite the general 'answers in simplest form' instruction.

components.component: Recognizes a computed result has a common factor between numerator and denominator, and reduces it to lowest terms
components.evidence: Items 4-8's correct sums/differences (5/6, 7/12, 1 1/12, 1 7/12, 5/12) are all already in lowest terms; the general Part B instruction 'Answers in simplest form' is never actually triggered by any item's arithmetic, so no item exercises this step even though the assessment's own instructions call for it.

gate1_components.carried_forward: Recognizes a computed result has a common factor between numerator and denominator, and reduces it to lowest terms
gate1_components.why: This component is the entire claim as stated. It belongs directly to the inference, nothing indicates it is assessed elsewhere, and its absence means the claim has zero supporting evidence rather than a narrower slice of support.

gate2_materiality.why: The teacher names G5C2a as a distinct, confirmed claim and the general 'simplest form' instruction implies it is being checked; a teacher scoring this assessment could easily believe simplification is being evidenced when in fact no item's numbers ever require it, so the gap is one the teacher would not otherwise notice.

gate3_value.why: A single short item with a deliberately reducible result closes a claim that currently has zero supporting evidence, at low added time and scoring cost; the value of moving from no evidence to independent evidence for a named claim clearly exceeds the burden of one more short item.

minimum_additional_observation.item_text: 10. 1/6 + 1/3 = ______. Write your answer in simplest form. Show your work.
minimum_additional_observation.variant_rule: Keep the unlike-denominator addition (or subtraction) format already practiced in Part B; choose numerators and denominators so the computed sum or difference has a numerator and denominator sharing a common factor greater than 1, so reduction is actually required. Keep the unreduced result a proper (non-mixed, non-improper) fraction so the item isolates simplification without also pulling in the improper-to-mixed regrouping tested by G5C2b. Vary the specific pair per class period or form so the numbers are not shared among students in advance; avoid denominators or numerators used elsewhere on this assessment.
minimum_additional_observation.conditions: Administered under the same declared conditions as the rest of the assessment: proctored_in_class, individual, AI prohibited_and_enforced, paper and pencil only.
minimum_additional_observation.sufficiency_line: Credit requires both the unreduced common-denominator result shown as a step (e.g. 3/6) and the correctly reduced final answer (1/2); a bare final answer with no visible reduction step does not confirm the reduction was a deliberate, understood step rather than a guess.

items.elicits: Recognizes the fractional-part sum (13/12) is improper, converts it to a whole number plus a proper fraction, and combines that whole number with the existing whole-number parts to state a final mixed number.
Recognizes the sum of the two fractions (19/12) is improper and regroups it into a mixed number as the final stated answer to the word problem.

claims.supports: A teacher may conclude the student can convert an improper fraction result to a mixed number, both within a pure mixed-number addition (item 6) and as the final step of a word problem (item 7), under supervised, novel-number conditions.
does_not_support: Does not test regrouping in the other direction (decomposing/'borrowing' from a whole number before subtracting, e.g. when a mixed minuend's fraction is smaller than the subtrahend's); the subtraction items (5, 8) do not require this since neither minuend needs borrowing.

Does not isolate the regrouping step from the preceding common-denominator addition step; an incorrect final mixed number could stem from either an equivalent-fraction error (G5C2core) or a regrouping error, and the artifact as given does not separate them at the scoring level.

A correct final mixed-number answer alone, without inspecting the shown steps, risks being read as regrouping mastery when it could reflect a memorized answer format; the 'show every step' requirement mitigates but does not eliminate this without a rubric that isolates the regroup step.

Only one regrouping context per item type (addition-produced improper result) is exercised; this is adequate for the claim as worded but should not be over-read as covering every situation in which regrouping arises.

delegation.reason: Proctored, individual, paper/pencil-only, no-AI conditions make it implausible for the regrouping step to be produced without the student performing it.

components.component: Recognizes a fractional sum is improper (numerator at or above denominator)
components.evidence: Both items produce an improper fractional sum (13/12 and 19/12) that the student must notice and convert.

components.component: Converts the improper fraction into a whole number plus a proper fraction
components.evidence: Both items require this conversion as the route to a mixed-number final answer.

components.component: Combines the regrouped whole number with any pre-existing whole-number part (mixed + mixed context)
components.evidence: Item 6 is an addition of two mixed numbers, requiring the regrouped whole number to be added to the existing whole-number parts.

components.component: Regroups in the subtraction/borrowing direction (decomposing a mixed minuend)
components.evidence: G5C2b's wording concerns converting an improper fraction RESULT to a mixed number; borrowing to enable a subtraction is a different regrouping direction not named in this claim, and neither subtraction item (5, 8) needs it since both minuends have sufficient numerators without borrowing.

gate1_components.why: The only unexercised regrouping direction (borrowing before subtracting) is not part of G5C2b's stated wording; the two named behaviors (recognizing an improper result and converting it to a mixed number) are both exercised, including in a mixed-number-plus-mixed-number context, by items 6 and 7.

gate2_materiality.why: Not reached: Gate 1 found no component belonging to this claim that is absent.

gate3_value.why: Not reached: Gate 1 found no component belonging to this claim that is absent.

claims.why_no_intervention: Gate 1 failed: both components named by G5C2b's wording are exercised by items 6 and 7; the only unexercised regrouping direction (subtraction borrowing) is a different skill not named in this claim.

items.elicits: Identifies that the shown incorrect work added the denominators, states why that produces a wrong-sized part (unlike-sized pieces cannot be combined by adding their denominators), and computes the correct sum via a valid common-denominator method.

claims.supports: A teacher may conclude the student can recognize the 'added the denominators' error in an unfamiliar incorrect solution, articulate why it produces a wrong-sized part, and independently produce the correct sum, under supervised, novel-number conditions.
does_not_support: Tests recognition and repair of only the one misconception named in the claim (adding denominators); it does not confirm diagnosis of other unlike-denominator errors, such as adding numerators and denominators separately without ever converting to like size, or subtracting without a common denominator.

The 'explain what the student did wrong' wording does not itself force the explanation to name the size-of-part mechanism; a vague response ('they did it wrong') paired with a correct repaired sum could otherwise be misread as full evidence unless scoring specifically checks for the mechanistic reason.

The 'explain' half and the 'show the correct answer' half of the claim can be completed with different levels of quality on the same response; a strong repair with a weak explanation (or vice versa) should be read as partial, not full, evidence of the whole claim.

Confirms the student can spot this misconception in someone else's work; it does not by itself confirm the student would not privately make this error in their own independent computation, though items 4-8 (all correctly executed with common denominators) speak to that separately.

delegation.reason: Proctored, individual, no-AI, paper/pencil-only conditions require the explanation and the repaired sum to be produced live by the student.

components.component: Locates the specific error in the shown incorrect work (adding denominators)
components.evidence: Item 9 presents 1/2 + 1/4 = 2/6 and asks the student to explain what went wrong.

components.component: States the mechanistic reason the error produces a wrong-sized part
components.evidence: The prompt 'Explain what the student did wrong' calls directly for this reasoning, matching the claim's own wording.

components.component: Produces the correct sum via a valid method
components.evidence: The prompt explicitly also asks the student to 'show the correct answer.'

gate1_components.why: No component of G5C3 is absent or not called for; all three named behaviors are exercised together by item 9, which matches the claim's wording closely (the same specific misconception, 'adding denominators,' named in both).

gate2_materiality.why: Not reached: Gate 1 found no absent component.

gate3_value.why: Not reached: Gate 1 found no absent component.

claims.why_no_intervention: Gate 1 failed: item 9 already exercises every component of G5C3 as stated, and its incorrect-solution scenario is the exact misconception named in the claim.

conditions_echo: Grade 5 Mathematics, end of Unit 4, summative, 25 minutes, individual, proctored_in_class supervision, AI prohibited_and_enforced, paper and pencil only; item formats have been practiced but these specific numbers/problems are new to students.
reviewer_notes: Under proctored, individual, no-AI, paper/pencil conditions, delegation risk is low across every claim this assessment carries; the interesting findings here are about coverage, not authorship. Four of the five claims (G5C1, G5C2core, G5C2b, G5C3) are already carried by items that exist on the page, each surviving Gate 1 with no material absence. The one exception is G5C2a: the assessment's own instruction says 'answers in simplest form,' but every correct result on the page (5/6, 7/12, 1 1/12, 1 7/12, 5/12) already happens to be in lowest terms, so the reduction step named by G5C2a is never actually triggered by the chosen numbers. A single added item with a deliberately reducible result would close that gap cheaply. Separately, because Part A (items 1-3) explicitly allows a benchmark or visual-model strategy instead of a common denominator, a teacher should not read a comparison item's shown work as automatic evidence for G5C2core specifically -- that overlap is worth remembering when scoring, not when redesigning the instrument.
